Where in the app: Labs › Electrolytes
Content to review: Normal 135–145 mEq/L; critical 120 / 160. High (Hypernatraemia): Water loss without access to water (elderly, intubated); Diabetes insipidus; Osmotic diuresis; Hypertonic saline or bicarbonate — Water leaves cells: brain cells shrink → confusion, seizures, tearing of bridging veins.. Low (Hyponatraemia): SIADH (pain, nausea, drugs, lung/brain disease); Heart, liver or kidney failure; Thiazides; Excess free water, beer potomania — Water moves into cells: brain swells inside a rigid skull → headache, vomiting, seizures, herniation.

Where in the app: Labs › Electrolytes
Content to review: Normal 3.5–5 mEq/L; critical 2.5 / 6.5. High (Hyperkalaemia): Kidney failure; ACE-i/ARB, spironolactone, trimethoprim; Cell breakdown: rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis, haemolysis; Acidosis, insulin deficiency (DKA) — shift out of cells — Resting potential rises toward threshold: peaked T → long PR, flat P → wide QRS → sine wave → VF or asystole.. Low (Hypokalaemia): Diuretics; Vomiting, diarrhoea; Insulin, β₂-agonists, alkalosis (shift in); Low magnesium — Hyperpolarised, slow-repolarising cells: flat T, U waves, arrhythmias (especially with digoxin), weakness, ileus.

Where in the app: Labs › Electrolytes
Content to review: Normal 98–107 mEq/L. High (Hyperchloraemia): Large volumes of 0.9 % saline; Diarrhoea (HCO₃⁻ loss); Renal tubular acidosis — Normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.. Low (Hypochloraemia): Vomiting / NG suction; Loop and thiazide diuretics; Chronic respiratory acidosis compensation — Maintains metabolic alkalosis — the kidney cannot excrete HCO₃⁻ without chloride.

Where in the app: Labs › Electrolytes
Content to review: Normal 22–29 mEq/L; critical 10 / 40. High (Metabolic alkalosis (or compensation)): Vomiting, diuretics; Compensation for chronic CO₂ retention; Bicarbonate / citrate load — Alkalaemia: low ionised calcium and potassium, arrhythmias, hypoventilation.. Low (Metabolic acidosis (or compensation)): Lactate, ketones, toxins, uraemia (gap); Diarrhoea, saline, RTA (non-gap); Compensation for chronic hyperventilation — Acidaemia: Kussmaul breathing, poor cardiac contractility, vasodilatation, hyperkalaemia.

Where in the app: Labs › Electrolytes
Content to review: Normal 1.12–1.32 mmol/L; critical 0.8 / 1.6. High (Hypercalcaemia): Hyperparathyroidism; Cancer (bone metastases, PTHrP); Vitamin D excess, thiazides — "Stones, bones, groans, moans": short QT, dehydration from nephrogenic DI, confusion.. Low (Hypocalcaemia): Massive transfusion (citrate); Sepsis, pancreatitis; Low magnesium, hypoparathyroidism; Alkalosis (more binding to albumin) — Neuromuscular irritability — tingling, tetany, laryngospasm, seizures; long QT; hypotension; poor clotting.

Where in the app: Labs › Electrolytes
Content to review: Normal 1.7–2.3 mg/dL. High (Hypermagnesaemia): Kidney failure; Magnesium infusion (pre-eclampsia) — Loss of reflexes, hypotension, respiratory depression, heart block.. Low (Hypomagnesaemia): Alcohol, malnutrition; Diuretics, PPIs; Diarrhoea, refeeding — Long QT and torsades; refractory low potassium and calcium.

Where in the app: Labs › Electrolytes
Content to review: Normal 2.5–4.5 mg/dL. High (Hyperphosphataemia): Kidney failure; Tumour lysis, rhabdomyolysis — Binds calcium → hypocalcaemia and calcium-phosphate deposition.. Low (Hypophosphataemia): Refeeding syndrome; DKA treatment; Alcohol, respiratory alkalosis — No ATP: diaphragm weakness, failure to wean, haemolysis, heart failure.

Where in the app: Labs › Kidney
Content to review: Normal 7–20 mg/dL. High (Raised BUN): Reduced GFR (AKI, CKD); Dehydration (more reabsorption); GI bleeding, steroids, high protein feeds — Uraemia: nausea, pericarditis, platelet dysfunction, encephalopathy.. Low (Low BUN): Liver failure; Malnutrition; Overhydration, pregnancy — Usually a clue, not a problem.

Where in the app: Labs › Kidney
Content to review: Normal 0.6–1.2 mg/dL. High (Raised creatinine): AKI: pre-renal, intrinsic (ATN), obstruction; CKD; High muscle mass, some drugs (trimethoprim) — Signals falling GFR: drug accumulation, fluid, potassium and acid retention.. Low (Low creatinine): Low muscle mass (elderly, amputees, critical illness); Pregnancy — May hide real kidney impairment.

Where in the app: Labs › Kidney
Content to review: Normal 90–130 mL/min/1.73m². Low (Low eGFR): CKD; AKI (unreliable until creatinine is steady) — Adjust drug doses; watch K⁺, acid and fluid.

Low (Hypoglycaemia): Insulin or sulfonylureas; Liver failure, sepsis, alcohol; Adrenal insufficiency — Neuroglycopenia: confusion, seizures, coma; sympathetic surge (sweating, tachycardia).

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › One equation runs the ventilator › The equation of motion
Content to review: Every pressure on a ventilator screen comes from one equation. Airway pressure equals resistance times flow, plus volume divided by compliance, plus PEEP. The ventilator is pushing gas through a tube and a tree of airways, and stretching an elastic lung that already sits at PEEP. Watch the lungs: each breath, the bases move down with the diaphragm.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › One equation runs the ventilator › Square flow, rising pressure
Content to review: In volume control with a square wave, flow is constant during inspiration. Look at the pressure trace. It jumps up the instant flow starts. That jump is resistance times flow. After the jump, pressure keeps climbing in a straight line, because as volume goes in, the elastic lung pushes back harder. The top of that climb is the peak inspiratory pressure, PIP.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › One equation runs the ventilator › Stop the flow: plateau
Content to review: Now an inspiratory hold. The valves close and flow drops to zero. With no flow, the resistance term disappears, so the pressure falls from the peak to a plateau. What is left is purely elastic: how hard the stretched lung and chest wall are pushing back. That is the plateau pressure. The drop from peak to plateau tells you about the airways. The plateau tells you about the lung.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › One equation runs the ventilator › Driving pressure and compliance
Content to review: Plateau minus PEEP is the driving pressure. It is the pressure needed to fit this tidal volume into this lung. Divide the tidal volume by the driving pressure and you get static compliance. Normal is about sixty to eighty milliliters per centimeter of water. The coloured bar under the numbers splits the peak pressure into its three parts: PEEP, elastic, and resistive.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › One equation runs the ventilator › Passive exhalation and tau
Content to review: Expiration is passive. The lung empties like a spring through a narrow tube, so flow is highest at the start and decays exponentially. The time constant, tau, is resistance times compliance. After one tau, about sixty three percent of the breath is out. After three tau, about ninety five percent. Here tau is under half a second, so the lung is empty long before the next breath.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Resistance or compliance? › Narrow airways
Content to review: This is severe bronchospasm. The airways in the translucent lungs are narrowed and inflamed. Look at the pressure: the peak is high, but the plateau after the pause is almost normal. The gap between them is huge. Resistance has gone up, compliance has not. The pressure is being spent pushing gas through the airways, not stretching the alveoli.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Resistance or compliance? › Open the airways
Content to review: A bronchodilator relaxes the smooth muscle. Airway resistance depends on the fourth power of the radius, so a small increase in calibre makes a large drop in resistance. Watch the airways widen, and the peak pressure fall toward the plateau. Time is compressed here: fifteen minutes of drug effect in about fifteen seconds.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Resistance or compliance? › A stiff lung
Content to review: Now a stiff, injured lung. Peak and plateau have both risen, and the gap between them is normal. The same tidal volume needs much more pressure to fit, because a large part of the lung is collapsed and the rest is stiff. That is a compliance problem.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Resistance or compliance? › The rule
Content to review: So, when the high-pressure alarm sounds, do an inspiratory hold. High peak with a normal plateau means resistance: kinked or bitten tube, secretions, bronchospasm. High peak with a high plateau means compliance: pneumothorax, mainstem intubation, pulmonary oedema, abdominal distension, or a stiff chest wall.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Volume control vs pressure control › Volume control
Content to review: In volume control you choose the tidal volume and the flow. The ventilator guarantees them, and pressure is whatever it takes. If the lung gets stiffer, or the airway narrows, pressure rises. That protects minute ventilation, but you must watch the pressures.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Volume control vs pressure control › Pressure control
Content to review: In pressure control you choose the pressure above PEEP and the inspiratory time. The pressure trace is now a square. Flow is high at first, then decays as the lung fills and the pressure difference shrinks. Tidal volume is the result. Here it is similar to before.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Volume control vs pressure control › Make the lung stiff
Content to review: Same pressure control settings, but now in a stiff ARDS lung. The pressure is capped, so the volume falls. Look at the tidal volume: much smaller. In pressure modes, a falling tidal volume is your warning sign, just as a rising pressure is in volume modes.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Volume control vs pressure control › Decelerating flow
Content to review: Volume control can also use a decelerating flow pattern. It delivers the volume with a lower peak pressure and a more even distribution between fast and slow lung units. The plateau does not change, because the volume and the lung are the same.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › PEEP, recruitment and overdistension › The collapsed, dependent lung
Content to review: This patient lies on their back. In ARDS, the heavy, wet lung collapses under its own weight, so the posterior, dependent regions are dark and airless. Blood still flows past them, but it picks up no oxygen. That is shunt, and it is why this patient is hypoxic despite a high FiO₂.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › PEEP, recruitment and overdistension › Raise PEEP
Content to review: Now raise PEEP to fourteen. Collapsed units need a higher pressure to open than to stay open. As PEEP rises, the dark posterior lung turns pink: those units are recruited. The same tidal volume now goes into more alveoli, so the driving pressure falls and compliance improves. Watch the oxygen saturation climb as shunt falls.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › PEEP, recruitment and overdistension › Too much
Content to review: Now PEEP twenty two. The anterior lung, which was already open, turns pale: it is over-stretched. The pressure volume loop flattens at the top, compliance falls again, and the plateau is above thirty. High intrathoracic pressure also squeezes the great veins, so venous return and blood pressure fall. More PEEP is not always better.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › PEEP, recruitment and overdistension › Find the middle
Content to review: The best PEEP opens the collapsed lung without over-stretching the open lung. At the bedside we look for the lowest driving pressure, an acceptable plateau, and oxygenation, while watching blood pressure. Try it yourself in explore mode.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Auto-PEEP and the time constant › Flow that never reaches zero
Content to review: In severe asthma the time constant is long. Look at the expiratory flow: it is still negative when the next breath begins. The lung has not finished emptying. Each breath leaves a little gas behind, until the lung sits at a higher volume. That trapped gas has pressure: intrinsic PEEP, or auto-PEEP.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Auto-PEEP and the time constant › Measure it
Content to review: An expiratory hold closes the valves at the end of expiration. The trapped alveolar pressure equilibrates with the airway, and the pressure rises above set PEEP. The difference is auto-PEEP. It adds to plateau pressure, compresses the heart, and makes the patient work harder to trigger.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Auto-PEEP and the time constant › Give it time
Content to review: The most powerful fix is expiratory time. Lower the rate, and shorten inspiration with a higher flow. Now expiratory flow reaches zero before the next breath, and the auto-PEEP disappears. Carbon dioxide may rise. In asthma that is usually accepted: permissive hypercapnia.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Triggering, cycling and dyssynchrony › Pressure support
Content to review: In pressure support the patient starts every breath. The red dashed line is the patient’s own muscle effort, which the ventilator cannot see directly. When the effort pulls enough flow past the trigger threshold, the ventilator delivers a set pressure. It stops when flow has fallen to a set percentage of the peak flow: the cycle-off criterion.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Triggering, cycling and dyssynchrony › Premature cycling
Content to review: Here the cycle-off threshold is sixty percent. The breath ends while the red effort line is still rising: the patient is still inhaling, but the ventilator has stopped. Look for the dip in expiratory flow right after cycling, and sometimes a second breath.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Triggering, cycling and dyssynchrony › Delayed cycling
Content to review: In COPD the flow decays slowly. With a cycle-off of five percent, the ventilator keeps inflating long after the patient has finished. The effort line goes negative: the patient is actively pushing to exhale against the machine. Raising the cycle-off percentage fixes it.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Triggering, cycling and dyssynchrony › Ineffective efforts
Content to review: Now watch the expiratory flow between breaths. Small upward bumps appear with each red effort, but no breath follows. Trapped gas means the patient must first overcome auto-PEEP before any flow reaches the sensor. These are ineffective efforts. Try the challenges to diagnose and fix each dyssynchrony yourself.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Oxygen: from air to mitochondria › Fresh gas in the alveolus
Content to review: Room air is twenty one percent oxygen. By the time it is warmed, humidified and mixed with carbon dioxide in the alveoli, the alveolar oxygen pressure is about one hundred. The alveolar gas equation says it: FiO₂ times seven hundred and thirteen, minus PaCO₂ divided by zero point eight.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Oxygen: from air to mitochondria › Blood arrives venous
Content to review: Here is one alveolar sac and its capillary basket, drawn to scale. Blood arrives from the pulmonary artery dark, about seventy percent saturated. It spreads over the alveoli in a single layer of red cells, separated from the air by a barrier thinner than one micrometre. It leaves bright red, about ninety seven percent saturated, through the pulmonary venule.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Oxygen: from air to mitochondria › Loading in the first third
Content to review: Zoom in to a single capillary. Red cells squeeze through one at a time. They take about three quarters of a second to cross, but they are fully loaded in the first third of that time. That reserve is why a healthy person can exercise without desaturating.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Oxygen: from air to mitochondria › Delivery and extraction
Content to review: In the muscle, arterial blood gives up oxygen to the mitochondria and picks up carbon dioxide. Oxygen delivery is arterial content times cardiac output: about a thousand millilitres a minute. The tissues use about a quarter of it, so venous blood returns about seventy five percent saturated.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Oxygen: from air to mitochondria › Anaemia: normal SpO₂, empty blood
Content to review: Now drop the haemoglobin to six and a half. Look at the arterial gas: PaO₂ and saturation are unchanged, and the pulse oximeter still reads normal. But oxygen content has halved, because content is one point three four times haemoglobin times saturation, plus a tiny dissolved fraction. The tissues must extract more, so venous saturation falls. SpO₂ tells you how full each lorry is, not how many lorries there are.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Why is the PaO₂ low? › Hypoventilation
Content to review: First, hypoventilation. Depress the drive, as an opioid would. Less fresh gas reaches the alveoli, so carbon dioxide builds up and, by the alveolar gas equation, alveolar oxygen falls. The lungs themselves are normal, so the A to a gradient stays normal. A little oxygen, or simply more ventilation, fixes it.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Why is the PaO₂ low? › V/Q mismatch
Content to review: Now V Q mismatch. Some alveoli get plenty of blood but little air. Blood leaving them is poorly oxygenated, and the A to a gradient widens. This is the commonest cause of hypoxaemia: pneumonia, COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Why is the PaO₂ low? › Oxygen fixes V/Q mismatch
Content to review: Raise the FiO₂ to forty percent. Even poorly ventilated alveoli eventually fill with oxygen-rich gas, so their blood saturates and the PaO₂ rises a lot. V Q mismatch is oxygen responsive.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Why is the PaO₂ low? › Shunt does not respond
Content to review: Now shunt: blood passing collapsed or flooded alveoli that receive no gas at all. The dark alveoli are airless, and the blood through them stays venous. Even at one hundred percent oxygen, the PaO₂ barely rises, because extra oxygen never reaches that blood. Shunt needs the alveoli reopened: PEEP, recruitment, treating the cause.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Why is the PaO₂ low? › Dead space
Content to review: Finally, dead space: alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused, shown with grey empty capillaries. They waste ventilation, so carbon dioxide clearance falls and the gap between PaCO₂ and end tidal CO₂ widens. Pulmonary embolism, low cardiac output and over-distension all do this.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › CO₂, pH and the kidneys › Acute respiratory acidosis
Content to review: This patient has taken an opioid. Carbon dioxide has risen to the eighties, and the pH has fallen quickly. Carbon dioxide combines with water to form carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions. Haemoglobin and proteins buffer some of them, so bicarbonate rises only about one per ten millimetres of mercury. That is acute compensation.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › CO₂, pH and the kidneys › The acid–base map
Content to review: Look at the acid base map. The dot sits in the acute respiratory acidosis band. Now we will keep the ventilation the same and let two days pass.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › CO₂, pH and the kidneys › 48 hours later
Content to review: The kidneys have been excreting acid as ammonium and reclaiming and making new bicarbonate. Bicarbonate has risen by about three and a half per ten millimetres of mercury, and the pH is back near normal, even though the CO₂ has not changed. The dot has moved along its path into the chronic band. This is why a COPD patient can live with a PaCO₂ of sixty.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › CO₂, pH and the kidneys › Post-hypercapnic alkalosis
Content to review: Now reverse the opioid. Ventilation returns, and CO₂ falls within minutes. But the kidneys need days to give back the extra bicarbonate, so the patient becomes alkalaemic. The same thing happens when a chronic retainer is over-ventilated on a ventilator.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Metabolic acidosis and the anion gap › Ketoacids consume bicarbonate
Content to review: Diabetic ketoacidosis. Ketoacids release hydrogen ions, and bicarbonate is used up buffering them. The ketone anions stay behind, unmeasured, so the anion gap, sodium minus chloride plus bicarbonate, widens. This is a high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Metabolic acidosis and the anion gap › The lungs compensate
Content to review: The low pH drives deep, fast breathing, Kussmaul respiration. Winter’s formula predicts the expected PaCO₂: one and a half times bicarbonate plus eight, plus or minus two. If the measured CO₂ is higher, the patient is tiring or sedated: a second, respiratory, problem.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Metabolic acidosis and the anion gap › Lactate
Content to review: In septic shock, lactate rises. Some comes from tissues short of oxygen, shown in magenta, but much comes from adrenaline-driven glycolysis and from a liver too poorly perfused to clear it. Lactate is a marker of stress and clearance, not simply of oxygen debt.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Metabolic acidosis and the anion gap › A mixed disorder
Content to review: Salicylate poisoning stimulates the respiratory centre directly, causing a respiratory alkalosis, and uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, adding organic acid. The CO₂ is lower than Winter’s formula predicts. Two primary disorders at once. The low CO₂ is protecting the patient: if they are intubated, it must stay low.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › ABG or VBG? › Two sampling sites
Content to review: An arterial gas samples blood on its way to the tissues. A venous gas samples blood that has already given up oxygen and collected carbon dioxide. In a stable patient, venous pH is about zero point zero three lower and venous CO₂ about five higher. Bicarbonate and lactate are almost the same.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › ABG or VBG? › Venous PO₂ is not oxygenation
Content to review: Venous PO₂ tells you only what the tissues left behind. A venous PO₂ of forty is normal, not hypoxaemia. To judge oxygenation, use the pulse oximeter or an arterial sample. The app always shows these two samples separately for that reason.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › ABG or VBG? › When they diverge
Content to review: During cardiac arrest with CPR, blood flow is so low that carbon dioxide piles up in the tissues. Venous CO₂ is far higher than arterial, and the venous pH far lower. When flow is poor, a venous gas no longer mirrors the arterial one.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Hyperkalaemia: stabilise, shift, remove › Potassium lives inside cells
Content to review: Almost all the body’s potassium is inside cells, about one hundred and forty inside against four outside. The sodium potassium pump in the membrane keeps it that way. That steep ratio sets the resting membrane potential of every heart cell, about minus eighty five millivolts.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Hyperkalaemia: stabilise, shift, remove › Raise the outside potassium
Content to review: Now the kidneys have failed and plasma potassium is seven point four. The ratio across the membrane falls, so the resting potential rises toward the threshold. Look at the gap on the membrane gauge: it has shrunk. The ECG shows peaked T waves, flattened P waves and a widening QRS. The heart is close to an arrhythmia.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Hyperkalaemia: stabilise, shift, remove › Step one: calcium
Content to review: Give intravenous calcium. Watch the numbers carefully: the potassium has not changed at all. What changed is the threshold. Calcium moves the threshold potential up, away from the resting potential, and restores the safety gap. The QRS narrows within minutes. Calcium buys time: thirty to sixty minutes.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Hyperkalaemia: stabilise, shift, remove › Step two: shift it into cells
Content to review: Now insulin with dextrose. Insulin switches on the sodium potassium pump, so potassium moves from the blood back into the cells. Plasma potassium falls by around one. Nebulised salbutamol does the same through beta two receptors. But nothing has left the body.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Hyperkalaemia: stabilise, shift, remove › The rebound
Content to review: Five hours later the insulin has worn off, the pumps have slowed, and potassium has leaked back out. This is the rebound. Shifting treatments are temporary. The potassium must be removed.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Hyperkalaemia: stabilise, shift, remove › Step three: remove it
Content to review: Dialysis removes potassium from the body, and so do binders, and diuretics if the kidneys work. Stabilise, shift, remove: in that order, and repeat the ECG and the potassium.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Hyponatraemia and the brain › Water follows solute
Content to review: Sodium is the main solute outside cells. Cell membranes let water through freely, so water moves until the concentration inside and outside is equal. Plasma sodium therefore sets the size of every cell, and the brain is the one organ that has no room to swell.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Hyponatraemia and the brain › Acute hyponatraemia
Content to review: Drop the sodium to one hundred and eighteen over a few hours, as happens with water intoxication or after surgery. Water rushes into brain cells and they swell. Inside the skull, that means headache, vomiting, seizures and eventually herniation. This is an emergency: a small bolus of hypertonic saline, raising the sodium by four to six, pulls water back out.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Hyponatraemia and the brain › The brain adapts
Content to review: If the sodium falls slowly, over days, brain cells export their own solutes, organic osmolytes, and shrink back to a normal size. This patient has the same sodium of one hundred and eighteen, but the brain cells are no longer swollen.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Hyponatraemia and the brain › Correcting too fast
Content to review: Now correct that chronic hyponatraemia too quickly: sixteen in a day. The adapted brain cells cannot re-import their osmolytes fast enough, water is pulled out, and the myelin of the pons can be destroyed. Osmotic demyelination appears days later and may be permanent. Limit correction to about eight to ten in twenty four hours.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Anaemia: the oximeter cannot see it › Normal blood
Content to review: Here is a capillary full of red cells. Each one is packed with haemoglobin, and each haemoglobin is ninety seven percent saturated with oxygen. Oxygen content is about nineteen millilitres in every decilitre of blood.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Anaemia: the oximeter cannot see it › Half the red cells
Content to review: Now the haemoglobin is six and a half. There are half as many red cells, but each one is still fully saturated, so the pulse oximeter still reads ninety seven percent. The oxygen content has halved. The heart pumps faster to compensate and the tissues extract more, so venous saturation falls.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Anaemia: the oximeter cannot see it › Treat the content
Content to review: A unit of red cells raises the haemoglobin by about one gram per decilitre and restores content. Remember: a normal SpO₂ says the haemoglobin present is full, not that there is enough of it.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Lactate: made and cleared › A balance
Content to review: Every cell makes some lactate, and the liver and kidneys clear it. A normal level of about one simply means production and clearance are matched.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Lactate: made and cleared › Shock
Content to review: Now cardiac output falls in shock. Tissues short of oxygen turn more glucose into lactate, and a poorly perfused liver clears less. Lactate climbs. Adrenaline and sepsis raise it further, even when oxygen delivery is adequate, by speeding glycolysis.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Lactate: made and cleared › Resuscitation
Content to review: Restore perfusion and the balance reverses. Lactate falls over hours, as the liver clears it. A falling lactate is one of the best signs that resuscitation is working.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › From artery to monitor › A column of saline carries the pressure
Content to review: An arterial line is a short cannula in an artery — here the right radial — joined by stiff, saline-filled tubing to a pressure transducer. The fluid column transmits every pressure change to the transducer, which turns it into the waveform and the numbers on the monitor.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › From artery to monitor › The radial cannula
Content to review: A 20-gauge cannula sits in the radial artery at the wrist. A bag of saline squeezed to 300 mmHg pushes about 3 mL an hour through the line, so blood cannot back up and clot. The bag must stay above the patient’s systolic pressure.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › From artery to monitor › The central line
Content to review: The central venous catheter enters the right internal jugular vein and runs down through the superior vena cava. Its tip should sit at the cavo-atrial junction, where the SVC meets the right atrium. The pressure there is the central venous pressure — essentially right-atrial pressure.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › From artery to monitor › Inside the chest
Content to review: Watch the chambers. The atria contract just after each P wave, the ventricles after each QRS. The right atrium glows brighter as its pressure rises, and a pulse wave runs from the aorta to the wrist — it arrives about a tenth of a second after the heart ejects.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › From artery to monitor › One reference level for everything
Content to review: All the pressures are measured against one reference point: the phlebostatic axis — the fourth intercostal space in the mid-axillary line, roughly the level of the right atrium. The transducer’s air–fluid interface, the zeroing stopcock, must sit level with it.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Reading the arterial waveform › Each beat, drawn
Content to review: The steep upstroke is the left ventricle ejecting into the aorta. The rounded top is the systolic peak. As ejection ends the aortic valve snaps shut, making the dicrotic notch. Then pressure runs off through the arterioles until the next beat: that low point is the diastolic pressure.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Reading the arterial waveform › Wrist versus aorta
Content to review: The radial systolic peak is taller and spikier than in the central aorta and diastolic slightly lower, so the pulse pressure is wider — the wave steepens as it travels out to smaller, stiffer arteries. The mean pressure hardly changes, which is one reason MAP is the number to trust for decisions. Compare the columns in the table: radial versus central aorta.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Reading the arterial waveform › A low dicrotic notch
Content to review: This patient is in vasodilated septic shock. Resistance is so low that blood runs off before the valve even closes: the notch slides down toward the diastolic level, diastolic pressure falls and MAP is below 65.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Reading the arterial waveform › Vasopressor effect
Content to review: Norepinephrine restores vascular tone. Watch diastolic pressure and MAP climb and the notch rise back up the downstroke.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Reading the arterial waveform › Stiff arteries
Content to review: An older, hypertensive patient: the stiff aorta cannot stretch to absorb each stroke, and the reflected wave returns early, during systole. Systolic pressure climbs, diastolic falls, and the pulse pressure widens past 60 mmHg — with a late systolic shoulder.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Reading the CVP waveform › Three peaks, two descents
Content to review: The a wave follows the P wave: the atrium contracts. The small c wave comes just after the QRS, as the closing tricuspid valve bulges back into the atrium. The x descent is the atrium relaxing and the valve ring being pulled down. The v wave is the atrium filling against the closed valve, near the end of the T wave. The y descent is the valve opening and blood rushing into the ventricle.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Reading the CVP waveform › Breathing moves the whole trace
Content to review: The shaded bands are breaths in. Breathing spontaneously, each breath in lowers the pressure in the chest, so the whole CVP trace dips. The monitor’s number averages every phase, so it reads a little low.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Reading the CVP waveform › Measure it yourself
Content to review: The monitor is frozen. Drag across the CVP trace and read the pressure at end-expiration — just before a shaded breath begins — at the base of the c wave. That is the value to record. Compare it with the monitor’s mean.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Reading the CVP waveform › On the ventilator it flips
Content to review: With positive-pressure ventilation, inspiration raises the pressure in the chest, so the CVP rises with each breath. End-expiration is now the lowest part of the respiratory cycle — still just before the next breath. The rule stays the same: read at end-expiration.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Reading the CVP waveform › Cannon a waves
Content to review: Complete heart block: atria and ventricles beat independently. When the atrium happens to contract while the tricuspid valve is shut, the blood is pushed back up the jugular: a giant cannon a wave.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Reading the CVP waveform › No a wave in AF
Content to review: Atrial fibrillation: the atria quiver and never contract as one, so the a wave disappears. You see only c and v, and the arterial pulse varies with every irregular R-R interval.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Reading the CVP waveform › Giant c-v waves
Content to review: Severe tricuspid regurgitation: the right ventricle pumps backwards into the atrium in every systole. The x descent is filled in by a giant c-v wave that can look almost like a ventricular trace.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Levelling and zeroing › Levelled
Content to review: The transducers are level with the phlebostatic axis. Levelling and zeroing are different jobs: levelling sets the reference height; zeroing tells the monitor what atmospheric pressure reads.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Levelling and zeroing › Ten centimetres too low
Content to review: The transducer has slipped 10 cm below the axis. The extra 10 cm of saline adds 10 × 0.74 = 7.4 mmHg to every reading. An arterial MAP of 95 becomes 102 — but a CVP of 5 becomes 12, more than double. Low transducer, high reading.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Levelling and zeroing › Raising the head of the bed
Content to review: The line was levelled with the bed flat. Now the head of the bed goes up to 30 degrees: the chest — and the phlebostatic axis — rises about 27 cm, but the transducer on the pole stays where it was. Every pressure now reads about 20 mmHg high. Re-level after any change in bed height or position.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Levelling and zeroing › Zero to air
Content to review: Zeroing: turn the stopcock off to the patient and open to air, press zero, then turn it back. The monitor now knows what atmospheric pressure looks like at the level of the stopcock.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Levelling and zeroing › The classic mistake
Content to review: This line was zeroed while the stopcock was still open to the patient. The monitor subtracted the patient’s own pressure: the trace sits around zero and swings negative. The shape is right; the numbers are wrong. Zero again, open to air.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Damping and the square-wave test › An optimally damped line
Content to review: Pull the flush for a second and let go. The trace jumps to the bag pressure, drops back, bounces one and a half to two times, then the waveform resumes. That is an optimally damped system: trust the systolic and diastolic values.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Damping and the square-wave test › Underdamped: it rings
Content to review: Extra extension tubing and stopcocks lower the natural frequency of the line. Now the flush bounces many times, and each heartbeat sets the line ringing: a spiky systolic overshoot. Systolic reads too high, diastolic slightly low — MAP is the least affected. It gets worse at faster heart rates.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Damping and the square-wave test › A small bubble does the same
Content to review: A tiny air bubble is very compliant. It drops the natural frequency sharply, so the line resonates and overshoots. Turn the stopcock off to the patient and flush the bubble out through the side port to waste.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Damping and the square-wave test › Overdamped: it smears
Content to review: A clot at the tip, a kink, a large bubble or a soft pressure bag absorbs the pulse. The flush slides back with no bounce, the notch disappears, systolic reads low and diastolic high. MAP still holds — until the line blocks completely.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Damping and the square-wave test › Never flush a clot forward
Content to review: An overdamped arterial line with sluggish blood return: aspirate first, then flush. Flushing a clot forward can embolise into the hand; flushing a bubble toward the patient puts air into the circulation — from a radial line it can even travel back up to the brain. Always clear air out of the side port to waste.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Heart–lung interactions › Pulse-pressure variation
Content to review: This patient has lost blood and is on the ventilator. Each positive-pressure breath squeezes blood out of the lungs into the left heart, then limits venous return for the next few beats. An underfilled heart is sensitive to that: the pulse pressure swings by more than 13 %.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Heart–lung interactions › Give fluid, watch PPV fall
Content to review: Three 500 mL boluses. Stroke volume rises, the heart moves up the steep part of its Starling curve onto the flat part, and the variation shrinks. The patient was fluid-responsive.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Heart–lung interactions › When PPV lies
Content to review: PPV only predicts fluid response with controlled breaths of at least 8 mL/kg, a regular rhythm, no spontaneous effort and a closed chest — and it is unreliable with very stiff lungs, RV failure or raised abdominal pressure. Here the patient breathes on their own: the variation is meaningless.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Heart–lung interactions › Irregular rhythm
Content to review: In atrial fibrillation every beat has a different filling time, so pulse pressure varies whatever the volume status. PPV cannot be used.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Heart–lung interactions › Pulsus paradoxus
Content to review: Cardiac tamponade, breathing spontaneously. The pericardium limits total heart volume: when the right heart fills on inspiration, the septum bows left and the left ventricle ejects less. Systolic pressure falls more than 10 mmHg with every breath in, the CVP is high, and there is no y descent.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Heart–lung interactions › Drain it
Content to review: Pericardiocentesis. As the fluid comes off, the paradox disappears, the CVP falls, the y descent returns and the heart rate slows.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Waveforms of disease › Aortic stenosis
Content to review: A narrow valve slows ejection: the upstroke is slow and late (pulsus tardus), the peak small (parvus), often with an anacrotic shoulder, and the notch is faint.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Waveforms of disease › Aortic regurgitation
Content to review: Blood falls back into the ventricle in diastole: diastolic pressure is very low, and the ventricle ejects a huge stroke — a steep upstroke, a wide pulse pressure, often a double systolic peak, and no notch.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Waveforms of disease › Failing left ventricle
Content to review: Cardiogenic shock: a weak ventricle ejects slowly against high resistance. The upstroke is sluggish, the pulse pressure narrow, and the CVP high. Little pulse-pressure variation: more fluid will not help.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Waveforms of disease › PVCs
Content to review: A premature beat fires before the ventricle has filled: a small or absent pulse. The pause that follows lets the next beat fill more, and it is bigger than normal.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Waveforms of disease › Right ventricular failure
Content to review: Massive pulmonary embolism: the right ventricle is pressure-loaded. The CVP is high with large a and v waves, the left heart is underfilled and the arterial pulse is narrow.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › ARDS: open the lung, keep it open, don’t overstretch it › A small, stiff, heavy lung
Content to review: Acute respiratory distress syndrome. The lungs are inflamed, heavy with protein-rich fluid, and the dependent regions at the back have collapsed. At a PEEP of five, look at how little of the lung is aerated.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › ARDS: open the lung, keep it open, don’t overstretch it › Down to the alveoli
Content to review: Zoom in to a cluster of alveoli. The upper units are open. The dependent ones at the bottom are collapsed or flooded, and blood keeps flowing past them.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › ARDS: open the lung, keep it open, don’t overstretch it › Shunt: blood that never meets air
Content to review: Follow the red cells past a collapsed alveolus: they leave as blue as they arrived. This is shunt. Extra oxygen cannot reach these units, which is why the saturation barely moves when you raise the FiO2.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › ARDS: open the lung, keep it open, don’t overstretch it › A thicker barrier, less surfactant
Content to review: Across the membrane, the interstitium is swollen and the lining fluid is thick. Surfactant is broken into islands, so alveoli collapse at the end of every breath.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › ARDS: open the lung, keep it open, don’t overstretch it › Raise the PEEP: recruitment
Content to review: Now drop the tidal volume to six millilitres per kilogram and raise the PEEP to sixteen. Pressure at end-expiration holds the dependent alveoli open. Collapsed units re-inflate, the shunt falls, and the blood leaving them turns red.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › ARDS: open the lung, keep it open, don’t overstretch it › Too much: overdistension
Content to review: Push PEEP to twenty-four and the least dependent alveoli are overstretched. Their walls thin, they compress the capillaries around them, and the plateau pressure climbs past thirty.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › ARDS: open the lung, keep it open, don’t overstretch it › The target
Content to review: The goal is in between: enough PEEP to keep the dependent lung open, small tidal volumes of about six millilitres per kilogram, a plateau below thirty and a driving pressure below fifteen. Watch the numbers as you choose.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › ARDS: open the lung, keep it open, don’t overstretch it › The film at PEEP five
Content to review: On a portable film at a PEEP of five, both lungs are white with patchy opacities and air bronchograms, and the heart is a normal size. That is the pattern of ARDS, not of heart failure.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › ARDS: open the lung, keep it open, don’t overstretch it › The film after recruitment
Content to review: At a PEEP of sixteen the same lungs look clearer, because collapsed units have opened and now hold air. The film changes with the ventilator settings, not only with the disease.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › ARDS: open the lung, keep it open, don’t overstretch it › The probe at PEEP five
Content to review: With a probe on the side of the chest at a PEEP of five, the B-lines merge into a white lung, and the dependent lung under the probe is consolidated and airless.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › ARDS: open the lung, keep it open, don’t overstretch it › The probe after recruitment
Content to review: At sixteen there are fewer B-lines and the consolidation has gone: the same recruitment you saw at the alveoli, seen at the bedside in seconds.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › ARDS vs asthma / COPD: stiff lung or narrow airway? › Peak = resistance + elastance + PEEP
Content to review: In volume control with constant flow, the peak pressure has three parts: PEEP, the pressure to stretch the lung — volume divided by compliance — and the pressure to push flow through the airways — resistance times flow. An inspiratory hold stops the flow, and what remains is the plateau.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › ARDS vs asthma / COPD: stiff lung or narrow airway? › ARDS: a compliance problem
Content to review: In ARDS the lung is small and stiff. Peak and plateau are both high and close together: the gap between them — the resistive part — is normal. The fix is about volume and PEEP: smaller breaths, keep the plateau under thirty.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › ARDS vs asthma / COPD: stiff lung or narrow airway? › Asthma: a resistance problem
Content to review: In severe asthma the airways are narrow. The peak pressure is very high, but the plateau is only modestly raised: the big peak-to-plateau gap is resistance. Raising the peak alarm will not help; opening the airways will.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › ARDS vs asthma / COPD: stiff lung or narrow airway? › Air trapping and auto-PEEP
Content to review: Look at the flow trace: expiratory flow has not returned to zero when the next breath starts. Gas is trapped. An expiratory hold measures the pressure it creates: auto-PEEP, on top of the set PEEP. Trapped gas raises intrathoracic pressure and can drop the blood pressure.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › ARDS vs asthma / COPD: stiff lung or narrow airway? › Treat the airway, give time to exhale
Content to review: A bronchodilator lowers resistance and a slower rate lengthens expiration. The peak falls, the gap narrows, expiratory flow reaches zero and the auto-PEEP melts away.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › ARDS vs asthma / COPD: stiff lung or narrow airway? › COPD: flow limitation
Content to review: In COPD the small airways collapse during expiration, limiting flow no matter how hard the patient pushes. The same rules apply: long expiratory times, modest minute ventilation, and measure the trapped pressure.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › ARDS vs asthma / COPD: stiff lung or narrow airway? › Two films, two problems
Content to review: The films tell the same story. The asthmatic lungs are hyperinflated: dark, over-expanded, with low flat diaphragms and a narrow heart, because trapped air cannot get out. The ARDS film was white.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › ARDS vs asthma / COPD: stiff lung or narrow airway? › The ultrasound difference
Content to review: On ultrasound the asthmatic lung slides, with A-lines only: full of air, with no fluid. The ARDS lung showed B-lines everywhere. A stiff lung and a narrow airway look different at the bedside.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Tension pneumothorax on the ventilator › Before
Content to review: A ventilated patient with normal lungs. Note the peak pressure, the saturation and the blood pressure.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Tension pneumothorax on the ventilator › Air under pressure
Content to review: A leak from the right lung lets air into the pleural space with every positive-pressure breath, and it cannot escape. Pleural pressure rises, the right lung collapses toward the hilum, and the mediastinum is pushed away.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Tension pneumothorax on the ventilator › Shunt and falling saturation
Content to review: Down at the alveoli, the compressed lung has collapsed but is still perfused: blood passes through without meeting air, and the saturation falls.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Tension pneumothorax on the ventilator › Obstructive shock
Content to review: The high intrathoracic pressure squeezes the great veins, venous return falls, and cardiac output with it. Peak pressures alarm high, the blood pressure drops and the heart races. This is obstructive shock: a mechanical problem that fluids and pressors cannot fix.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Tension pneumothorax on the ventilator › Decompress
Content to review: Needle decompression, then a chest tube. The pleural air escapes, the lung re-expands, peak pressure falls, venous return and blood pressure recover, and the saturation climbs.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Tension pneumothorax on the ventilator › What the probe would have shown
Content to review: Back to the moment before decompression, seen with a linear probe on the front of the chest. On the right the bright pleural line does not shimmer: no sliding, only A-line echoes, and the M-mode is a barcode. On the left the lung slides and the M-mode looks like a seashore. Ultrasound takes seconds, but it confirms — it should never delay decompression in a crashing patient.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Tension pneumothorax on the ventilator › What the film would have shown
Content to review: The same moment on a portable film: a pleural edge with no lung markings beyond it, a flattened right hemidiaphragm, and the mediastinum pushed to the left. A film like this is a teaching picture; tension is treated on clinical signs.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Tension pneumothorax on the ventilator › A lung point as the lung returns
Content to review: After decompression the tension is gone, but a little air is still trapped at the front of the chest. Anteriorly there is still no sliding. Move the probe laterally: at one spot sliding appears and disappears with each breath — a lung point, the edge of the remaining air. It confirms a pneumothorax, and it moves outward as the drain lets the lung come back.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Needle thoracostomy: site, rib, depth › Tension on the ventilator
Content to review: A ventilated patient with a right tension pneumothorax: high peak and plateau pressures, falling saturation, blood pressure collapsing. The treatment is to let the pleural air out — now.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Needle thoracostomy: site, rib, depth › Two sites
Content to review: Two recognised sites: the second intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line, and the fourth or fifth space at the anterior or mid-axillary line, inside the safe triangle. Stay lateral to the nipple line and above it.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Needle thoracostomy: site, rib, depth › Over the top of the rib
Content to review: Look at the rib above: its lower edge hides the intercostal vein, artery and nerve. A needle under the upper rib risks bleeding into the chest you are trying to decompress. Go over the top of the rib below.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Needle thoracostomy: site, rib, depth › Too short
Content to review: Anteriorly the needle crosses the pectoral muscles. In a heavier patient a five-centimetre catheter ends in muscle. No air, no change — and the attempt looks done when it is not.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Needle thoracostomy: site, rib, depth › Lateral, long enough: decompression
Content to review: At the fourth or fifth space laterally, with a longer catheter, over the rib below and perpendicular to the skin: a rush of air as the pleura is crossed. Stop there, advance the catheter off the needle. Watch the peak pressure, the saturation and the blood pressure recover.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Needle thoracostomy: site, rib, depth › Too medial, too low
Content to review: Too close to the sternum and you meet the internal thoracic artery, then the heart. Too low and the diaphragm, liver or spleen are in the way. Landmarks matter more than speed.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › Needle thoracostomy: site, rib, depth › A bridge, not a fix
Content to review: A needle is a bridge. Catheters kink and dislodge, and the tension can return. Reassess often, and follow with a finger thoracostomy or a chest drain.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › The child’s airway: radius to the fourth power › Radius to the fourth power
Content to review: A child’s airway is not just a smaller copy of an adult’s. It is narrower and softer, and resistance to flow depends on the radius raised to the fourth power. Halve the radius, and the resistance rises sixteen times.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › The child’s airway: radius to the fourth power › One millimetre of swelling
Content to review: Take one millimetre of swelling all the way round. In an adult airway of eight millimetres, the lumen falls to six, and resistance rises about three times. In an infant airway of four millimetres, it falls to two, and resistance rises sixteen times. The same swelling, a very different child.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › The child’s airway: radius to the fourth power › Crying makes it worse
Content to review: When a frightened child cries and gasps, flow through the narrowed segment turns turbulent, and the pressure needed rises with the fifth power of the radius: thirty two times. Keeping the child calm, on a parent’s lap, is part of the treatment.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › The child’s airway: radius to the fourth power › The narrowest ring
Content to review: Just below the vocal cords sits the cricoid, the only complete ring of cartilage in the airway. Swelling there, from infection or from a tube that is too big, has nowhere to go but inward.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › The child’s airway: radius to the fourth power › The same law in the tube
Content to review: The same law applies to the endotracheal tube. These lungs are healthy and unchanged; only the tube is smaller, seven millimetres instead of eight. Watch the peak pressure: the gap between peak and plateau, the pressure spent on resistance, grows.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › The child’s airway: radius to the fourth power › Six millimetres
Content to review: At six millimetres that resistive pressure has roughly tripled. A child’s tube may be three and a half millimetres, so a little secretion or a kink takes away a large share of its radius. That is why the tube is the first thing to check when a ventilated child deteriorates.

Where in the app: Ventilator › Learn › The child’s airway: radius to the fourth power › Back to eight
Content to review: Back to the eight millimetre tube, and the resistive gap closes. Check the tube, then the patient, then the machine.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Respiratory vs metabolic acidosis › Two buffers, two organs
Content to review: pH is set by the ratio of bicarbonate to carbon dioxide. The lungs control carbon dioxide within minutes; the kidneys control bicarbonate over days. Normal: pH seven point four, PaCO2 forty, bicarbonate twenty-four.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Respiratory vs metabolic acidosis › Acute respiratory acidosis
Content to review: An opioid overdose. Breathing slows, carbon dioxide accumulates, and the pH falls. Bicarbonate barely moves — about one for every ten of CO2 — because the kidneys have not had time. Watch the end-tidal CO2 and the respiratory rate: the cause is on the monitor.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Respiratory vs metabolic acidosis › Chronic: the kidneys catch up
Content to review: Leave the same hypoventilation for three days. The kidneys retain bicarbonate — about four for every ten of CO2 — and the pH climbs back toward normal while the CO2 stays high. That is renal compensation, and it takes days.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Respiratory vs metabolic acidosis › Metabolic acidosis
Content to review: Now a metabolic acidosis: twelve millimoles of acid added, bicarbonate used up to buffer it. Within minutes the lungs respond — deeper, faster breathing lowers the CO2. Expected PaCO2 is one and a half times the bicarbonate plus eight, give or take two.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Respiratory vs metabolic acidosis › When the lungs cannot compensate
Content to review: Put the same patient on a ventilator set to a normal minute ventilation. The compensation is taken away: CO2 rises back toward forty and the pH drops sharply. A metabolic acidosis on the ventilator needs a higher minute ventilation, not a normal one.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Respiratory vs metabolic acidosis › Reading the pattern
Content to review: First the pH: acid or alkaline. Then which value explains it: a high CO2 is respiratory, a low bicarbonate is metabolic. Then check the other value: is the compensation what you expect? If not, there is a second process.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › DKA: acid, water and potassium › No insulin
Content to review: Without insulin, cells cannot take up glucose, so the liver makes more and fat is broken down. Fatty acids are turned into ketoacids. Glucose is over five hundred; the patient is vomiting and breathing deeply.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › DKA: acid, water and potassium › An anion-gap acidosis
Content to review: Ketoacids use up bicarbonate. The unmeasured ketone anions widen the anion gap. The lungs compensate with Kussmaul breathing, driving the CO2 down.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › DKA: acid, water and potassium › Osmotic diuresis
Content to review: Glucose spills into the urine and drags water and sodium with it. By the time the patient arrives, several litres have been lost, and the kidneys are underperfused.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › DKA: acid, water and potassium › Potassium: high in the blood, low in the body
Content to review: Plasma potassium is high, because acidosis and the lack of insulin push potassium out of cells. But the diuresis has been washing it out for days: total-body potassium is low. Insulin will reveal the deficit.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › DKA: acid, water and potassium › Fluids first
Content to review: The first treatment is fluid. Volume restores perfusion and lets the kidneys clear glucose and ketones.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › DKA: acid, water and potassium › Insulin — and watch the potassium
Content to review: Insulin stops ketone production and moves potassium back into the cells. Glucose and the anion gap fall — and so does potassium, often below normal. Check it before insulin, and replace it: if potassium is low, give potassium first.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › DKA: acid, water and potassium › Close the gap
Content to review: Keep the insulin infusion running until the anion gap closes, adding dextrose as glucose falls. The glucose normalises long before the acidosis does.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Pregnancy: the normal blood gas that isn’t › The reference
Content to review: First, a non-pregnant adult breathing room air: a pH of seven point four, a carbon dioxide of forty, a bicarbonate of about twenty four.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Pregnancy: the normal blood gas that isn’t › Normal at term
Content to review: Now a healthy woman at thirty eight weeks. Progesterone makes the respiratory centre more sensitive, so she breathes more: carbon dioxide about thirty. Over weeks her kidneys excrete bicarbonate, down to about twenty, and the pH sits just above normal. For her, this is normal.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Pregnancy: the normal blood gas that isn’t › Why it helps the baby
Content to review: The low maternal carbon dioxide widens the gradient across the placenta, so the fetus can offload its own. Her oxygen is normal or a little high, because less carbon dioxide in the alveoli leaves room for more oxygen.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Pregnancy: the normal blood gas that isn’t › Thinner blood
Content to review: Plasma volume rises by nearly half and red cell mass by about a quarter, so haemoglobin falls to around eleven. Oxygen content is lower, and a higher cardiac output makes up the difference.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Pregnancy: the normal blood gas that isn’t › The trap: a normal carbon dioxide
Content to review: Now a pregnant woman with severe asthma. Her carbon dioxide reads in the forties, which looks normal, but her own normal is thirty. She is retaining carbon dioxide, and with little bicarbonate to buffer it, her pH has already fallen to about seven point three. She is tiring.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Pregnancy: the normal blood gas that isn’t › Act early
Content to review: Treat her as severe: bronchodilators, steroids and magnesium, senior help early, and keep her saturation at ninety five percent or more, because the baby’s oxygen depends on hers. As the airways open, her carbon dioxide falls back toward her own normal.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Apnoea: how long the oxygen lasts — child, newborn, pregnancy › The oxygen already on board
Content to review: When breathing stops, the body lives on the oxygen it already holds: a little in the blood, and the gas left in the lungs at the end of a breath, the functional residual capacity. Breathing room air, a healthy adult falls below ninety percent in about a minute.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Apnoea: how long the oxygen lasts — child, newborn, pregnancy › Pre-oxygenation fills the tank
Content to review: Breathing pure oxygen through a tight seal for three minutes washes the nitrogen out of that lung volume and replaces it with oxygen. Now the same adult stays above ninety percent for about eight minutes. Nothing else we do buys as much time.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Apnoea: how long the oxygen lasts — child, newborn, pregnancy › The cliff
Content to review: Look at the shape. The saturation hardly moves while the lung store drains, because the top of the dissociation curve is flat. Once alveolar oxygen falls to about sixty, the curve turns steep and the saturation falls off a cliff. Stop and re-oxygenate before the edge, not after it.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Apnoea: how long the oxygen lasts — child, newborn, pregnancy › Pregnancy
Content to review: At term the uterus pushes the diaphragm up, so the functional residual capacity is about a fifth smaller, while mother, placenta and baby consume more oxygen. The tank is smaller and drains faster: about five minutes instead of eight, and the baby shares the deficit.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Apnoea: how long the oxygen lasts — child, newborn, pregnancy › Obesity
Content to review: Lying flat, the weight of the abdomen and chest wall squeezes the lungs, and more tissue uses more oxygen. Even well pre-oxygenated, this patient may have under four minutes.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Apnoea: how long the oxygen lasts — child, newborn, pregnancy › The child
Content to review: A four year old uses nearly twice as much oxygen per kilo as an adult, from a smaller lung volume per kilo. Pre-oxygenated, the saturation holds for about three minutes. On room air, it is seconds.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Apnoea: how long the oxygen lasts — child, newborn, pregnancy › Infant and newborn
Content to review: Infants are faster still. Their soft chest wall lets the lung volume collapse once they are asleep or paralysed, and their oxygen use per kilo is the highest of any age. Under two minutes is typical. Fetal haemoglobin holds oxygen tightly, which helps the newborn a little, but the reserve is tiny.

Where in the app: Blood gas › Learn › Apnoea: how long the oxygen lasts — child, newborn, pregnancy › Buying time
Content to review: What buys time: a good seal and full pre-oxygenation, head-up positioning in obesity and pregnancy, oxygen flowing through the nose during the attempt, and a plan agreed beforehand: the time or saturation at which you stop, and ventilate.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Hyperkalaemia: the membrane, the ECG, the rescue › A membrane held at −85 mV
Content to review: Heart muscle cells hold about one hundred and forty millimoles of potassium inside, against about four outside. That gradient, leaking out through potassium channels, holds the resting membrane near minus eighty-five millivolts.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Hyperkalaemia: the membrane, the ECG, the rescue › The pump keeps the gradient
Content to review: The sodium potassium pump spends ATP to carry two potassium ions in for every three sodium ions out. Keep an eye on it; it becomes a treatment later.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Hyperkalaemia: the membrane, the ECG, the rescue › The kidneys fail and potassium climbs
Content to review: With the kidneys failing, plasma potassium rises. The outward leak weakens, the resting potential creeps toward threshold, and the ECG changes in order: tall peaked T waves, then a longer PR and flattened P waves, then a widening QRS.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Hyperkalaemia: the membrane, the ECG, the rescue › A sine wave is a pre-arrest rhythm
Content to review: Above about nine, the widened QRS runs into the T wave. This sine-wave pattern comes just before ventricular fibrillation or asystole.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Hyperkalaemia: the membrane, the ECG, the rescue › Stabilise: calcium
Content to review: Calcium goes in first. Potassium stays exactly where it was. Calcium raises the threshold potential, re-opening the gap between rest and threshold, and the QRS narrows within minutes. It buys roughly thirty to sixty minutes.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Hyperkalaemia: the membrane, the ECG, the rescue › Shift: insulin and dextrose
Content to review: Insulin with dextrose drives the sodium potassium pump harder, moving potassium back into cells. Plasma potassium falls by about one. Nebulised salbutamol works the same way. None of it has left the body.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Hyperkalaemia: the membrane, the ECG, the rescue › The rebound
Content to review: Hours later the insulin has worn off and potassium leaks back out of the cells. Shifting is temporary.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Hyperkalaemia: the membrane, the ECG, the rescue › Remove: dialysis
Content to review: Removal is the cure: dialysis, gut binders, or diuretics if the kidneys still work. Stabilise, shift, remove. Then repeat the ECG and the potassium.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Reversing anticoagulation: warfarin, heparin and clots that dissolve › Normal clotting
Content to review: When a vessel tears, platelets plug the hole, and clotting factors made by the liver generate thrombin, which weaves fibrinogen into a fibrin mesh. The trace shows a clot forming on time and staying firm.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Reversing anticoagulation: warfarin, heparin and clots that dissolve › Warfarin, INR over six
Content to review: Warfarin blocks the recycling of vitamin K, so the liver makes clotting factors that cannot work. Here only about seven percent of factors two, seven, nine and ten are active. The INR is over six, the clot forms late and weak, and this patient is bleeding.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Reversing anticoagulation: warfarin, heparin and clots that dissolve › Prothrombin complex concentrate
Content to review: Prothrombin complex concentrate replaces those four factors directly. Thirty minutes later the INR is close to normal and the clot forms on time.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Reversing anticoagulation: warfarin, heparin and clots that dissolve › A day later, without vitamin K
Content to review: But factor seven lasts only about six hours. Without vitamin K the liver still cannot make working factors, and a day later the INR has climbed back toward three.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Reversing anticoagulation: warfarin, heparin and clots that dissolve › With vitamin K
Content to review: Give intravenous vitamin K with the concentrate, and the liver takes over as the concentrate is used up. A day later the INR is still normal.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Reversing anticoagulation: warfarin, heparin and clots that dissolve › Heparin
Content to review: Heparin works differently. It supercharges antithrombin, which switches off thrombin and factor ten A. The INR hardly moves, but the aPTT is several times normal.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Reversing anticoagulation: warfarin, heparin and clots that dissolve › Protamine
Content to review: Protamine is strongly positive and binds the negative heparin chains. Within minutes the aPTT is back to normal. If an infusion were still running it would climb again, so stop the heparin first.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Reversing anticoagulation: warfarin, heparin and clots that dissolve › When clots dissolve
Content to review: Major trauma can switch on fibrinolysis: clots break down almost as fast as they form, and fibrinogen is consumed. The trace rises, then melts away, and fibrinogen falls toward one hundred.

Where in the app: Labs › Learn › Reversing anticoagulation: warfarin, heparin and clots that dissolve › Tranexamic acid, then fibrinogen
Content to review: Tranexamic acid stops plasminogen binding to fibrin, so clots hold; it works best within three hours of injury. Replacing fibrinogen, with cryoprecipitate or concentrate, restores the strength of the clot.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Shock states at the bedside › Four ways to fail
Content to review: Blood pressure is flow times resistance: mean arterial pressure is cardiac output times systemic vascular resistance, plus the venous pressure. Shock is inadequate tissue perfusion, and every type breaks a different part of that equation. This is a normal patient for comparison.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Shock states at the bedside › Distributive: the resistance falls
Content to review: Septic shock. Inflammatory mediators relax the arterioles, so resistance collapses. The heart speeds up and output is normal or high. On the arterial line the diastolic pressure is low, the pulse pressure is wide for the mean pressure, and the dicrotic notch sits low on the downstroke.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Shock states at the bedside › Norepinephrine restores tone
Content to review: After fluid, norepinephrine constricts the arterioles through alpha-1 receptors. Resistance rises, the diastolic pressure and mean pressure come up, and the heart rate barely changes. The target is a mean pressure of about sixty-five.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Shock states at the bedside › Cardiogenic: the pump fails
Content to review: Cardiogenic shock. A failing left ventricle ejects a small stroke volume, so the pulse pressure is narrow. Blood backs up: filling pressures and the CVP are high. Resistance rises as the body tries to hold the pressure, which makes the weak heart work harder.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Shock states at the bedside › Dobutamine: squeeze harder
Content to review: Dobutamine stimulates beta-1 receptors on the myocardium. Contractility and stroke volume rise and resistance falls a little, so cardiac output climbs. Pressure may not rise much; a vasopressor is often needed alongside. Fluids would only raise the CVP further.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Shock states at the bedside › Obstructive: tamponade
Content to review: Cardiac tamponade. Fluid in the pericardium squeezes the heart from outside, so the chambers cannot fill. The CVP is high, the pressures in all four chambers move toward the same value, and the stroke volume is small. The heart is fast, the pulse pressure narrow.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Shock states at the bedside › Pulsus paradoxus
Content to review: Watch the arterial trace with breathing. On inspiration the right heart fills, the septum bulges left, and the left ventricle fills even less: systolic pressure drops more than ten millimetres of mercury. That exaggerated fall is pulsus paradoxus.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Shock states at the bedside › Pericardiocentesis
Content to review: Draining even a small volume of pericardial fluid releases the heart. Filling recovers, the CVP falls, stroke volume and cardiac output return, and the paradox disappears.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Shock states at the bedside › Hypovolaemic: the tank is empty
Content to review: Haemorrhagic shock. With too little blood, venous return and preload fall: the CVP is low, the stroke volume small and the pulse pressure narrow. Resistance and heart rate rise to compensate. On the ventilator, each breath squeezes the small preload further, so the pulse pressure varies widely with breathing — a high pulse pressure variation.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Shock states at the bedside › Volume, then blood
Content to review: Give volume, and in haemorrhage give blood: it restores preload and oxygen-carrying capacity together. Stroke volume rises, the pulse pressure widens, the variation with breathing shrinks and the heart slows. Stopping the bleeding is the definitive treatment.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Shock states at the bedside › Read the pattern
Content to review: Low resistance with high output: distributive. Low output with high filling pressures: cardiogenic. High filling pressures with a heart that cannot fill: obstructive. Low output with low filling pressures: hypovolaemic. The monitor tells you which lever to pull.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Oxygen delivery: DO₂ = CO × CaO₂ › The equation
Content to review: Oxygen content is mostly haemoglobin carrying oxygen: one point three four times haemoglobin times saturation, plus a tiny dissolved amount. Delivery is content times cardiac output. Normally about a thousand millilitres a minute is delivered and a quarter is used, so venous blood returns about seventy-five percent saturated.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Oxygen delivery: DO₂ = CO × CaO₂ › Anaemia halves the content
Content to review: Halve the haemoglobin. The saturation is unchanged — the pulse oximeter looks perfect — but the oxygen content has halved. A healthy heart raises its output and thinner blood lowers the resistance, which recovers part of the delivery. The oximeter measures the percentage of haemoglobin that is full, not how much haemoglobin there is.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Oxygen delivery: DO₂ = CO × CaO₂ › A failing heart cannot compensate
Content to review: Give the same anaemia to a patient whose heart cannot raise its output. Now delivery falls far below what the tissues need: venous saturation drops and lactate starts to climb.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Oxygen delivery: DO₂ = CO × CaO₂ › Hypoxaemia lowers saturation
Content to review: Now keep the haemoglobin normal but add shunt in the lungs. The saturation falls, and content falls with it — but less than you might expect, because of the shape of the dissociation curve.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Oxygen delivery: DO₂ = CO × CaO₂ › Low output: cardiogenic shock
Content to review: With normal blood but a failing pump, delivery falls in proportion to the output. The tissues extract more, venous saturation falls, and lactate rises as cells switch to anaerobic metabolism.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Oxygen delivery: DO₂ = CO × CaO₂ › High delivery, still lactic: sepsis
Content to review: Septic shock can have a high cardiac output and high delivery, yet lactate is raised: blood is poorly distributed through the microcirculation, and the cells themselves use oxygen badly. A normal or high venous saturation does not rule out tissue hypoxia.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Haemorrhagic shock and transfusion › Before
Content to review: A healthy adult. Note the haemoglobin, the pressures, and the oxygen delivery.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Haemorrhagic shock and transfusion › Early: the haemoglobin lies
Content to review: Rapid bleeding. What is lost is whole blood, so the haemoglobin concentration is almost unchanged at first. The problem is volume: low preload, low CVP, small stroke volume, narrow pulse pressure, a fast heart and falling delivery.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Haemorrhagic shock and transfusion › Crystalloid dilutes
Content to review: Two litres of crystalloid restore some volume and pressure, but now the haemoglobin falls: the remaining red cells are diluted. Delivery improves less than the blood pressure suggests, and much of the crystalloid leaves the circulation within an hour.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Haemorrhagic shock and transfusion › Give blood
Content to review: Packed red cells restore volume and oxygen-carrying capacity together. Stroke volume and pulse pressure rise, the heart slows, the haemoglobin climbs and delivery improves. In major haemorrhage, give plasma and platelets with the red cells, and calcium.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Haemorrhagic shock and transfusion › Watch for a reaction
Content to review: During every unit, watch the patient. Fever, rigors, a sudden fall in pressure, wheeze, urticaria, back pain or dark urine suggest a reaction. Stop the transfusion, keep the line open with saline, check the patient and the product, and follow your transfusion protocol.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Haemorrhagic shock and transfusion › Stop the bleeding
Content to review: Transfusion buys time. Definitive treatment is control of the bleeding: pressure, tourniquet, surgery or interventional radiology.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Intra-aortic balloon pump timing › Why a balloon
Content to review: A failing left ventricle, low cardiac output. A balloon in the descending aorta inflates in diastole and deflates just before systole: it pushes blood back toward the coronaries while the heart relaxes, and leaves an emptier aorta for the next beat to eject into.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Intra-aortic balloon pump timing › Reading 1:2
Content to review: At one-to-two every other beat is assisted, so the trace compares itself. Find the unassisted systole, the dicrotic notch, then the diastolic augmentation — ideally as high as systole or higher.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Intra-aortic balloon pump timing › Two end-diastolic pressures
Content to review: Deflation drops the pressure just before the next beat: the balloon-assisted end-diastolic pressure should be lower than the patient’s own, and the assisted systole lower than the unassisted one. That is the afterload reduction.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Intra-aortic balloon pump timing › Early inflation
Content to review: Inflate too early and the balloon meets a ventricle that is still ejecting. The notch disappears, the aortic valve closes early and stroke volume falls.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Intra-aortic balloon pump timing › Late inflation
Content to review: Inflate late and you see the notch, then a gap, then a smaller augmentation. Less diastolic pressure means less coronary benefit.

Where in the app: Lines › Learn › Intra-aortic balloon pump timing › Early deflation
