Explanation: The shape is normal but the whole waveform is shifted down by about the patient’s own mean pressure. Zeroing with the stopcock open to the patient made the monitor treat the MAP as “zero”. Turn the stopcock off to the patient, open to air, zero, and turn it back.

Where in the app: Lines › Challenge › Blood in the tubing
Content to review: Blood has crept up the arterial tubing toward the transducer and the trace is becoming damped. The fast-flush only reaches about 90 mmHg. Answer: Pressure bag under-inflated — below arterial systolic. Other options: Transducer below the axis | Catheter in the vein | Underdamped system. Explanation: The flush bag must be at 300 mmHg — above systolic — or blood backs up the line, the continuous flush stops and the catheter clots. Inflate the bag to 300 and flush the blood back.

Where in the app: Lines › Challenge › The CVP that pulses to 25
Content to review: The CVP trace now swings from about 2 to 25 mmHg with every beat, and there are occasional ectopic beats. Freeze the monitor and look at the shape. Answer: The catheter tip has migrated into the right ventricle. Other options: Giant v waves from tricuspid regurgitation | Cannon a waves from heart block | An underdamped CVP line. Explanation: A sharp systolic rise to ≈ 25 and a diastolic floor near zero is a ventricular trace. TR can give a large c-v wave, but diastolic pressure stays high. Notify the provider and get a chest X-ray; stop vasoactive infusions through that lumen until the tip is confirmed. The provider withdraws it to the cavo-atrial junction; ectopy settles once the tip leaves the RV.

Where in the app: Lines › Challenge › Onto the transport stretcher
Item: Before changing the norepinephrine, what do you suspect?
Content to review: You have just moved the patient onto the transport stretcher. The arterial trace looks smudged and MAP reads higher than a minute ago. Norepinephrine 0.1 µg/kg/min is running. Find everything that is wrong before you touch the pump. Answer: A monitoring problem: the transducer was not re-levelled and the trace is damped. Other options: The septic shock has resolved | The norepinephrine dose is too high | Fluid overload. Explanation: A sudden change after moving a patient is a monitoring problem until proven otherwise. The transducer stayed at the old bed height (reading high), and the wrist is flexed, kinking the cannula (damped). Level, straighten the wrist, check with a flush test — then titrate to the real MAP.

Where in the app: Lines › Challenge › Six hours after cardiac surgery
Content to review: Six hours after valve surgery, the chest drains have stopped draining. Heart rate about 130. Look at both traces with the breathing. Answer: Cardiac tamponade. Other options: Hypovolaemia from bleeding | LV failure | Complete heart block. Explanation: High CVP (≈ 18) with no y descent, a narrow pulse pressure, and systolic falling more than 10 mmHg on each breath in (pulsus paradoxus): tamponade. Hypovolaemia would have a low CVP. Treatment: surgical re-exploration or pericardiocentesis.

Where in the app: Lines › Challenge › Slow and strange
Item: What causes the tall CVP waves?
Content to review: Heart rate 38. Every so often a very tall wave appears on the CVP trace. Answer: Cannon a waves: atria contracting against a closed tricuspid (AV dissociation). Other options: Giant v waves of tricuspid regurgitation | Catheter in the right ventricle | Artefact from coughing. Explanation: The tall waves are intermittent and fall where an independent P wave lands during ventricular systole: cannon a waves of complete heart block. The slow rate also gives large stroke volumes and a wide pulse pressure.

Where in the app: Lines › Challenge › A bounding pulse
Content to review: The arterial trace shows a steep upstroke, a very low diastolic pressure and no clear dicrotic notch. Answer: Aortic regurgitation. Other options: Aortic stenosis | Hypovolaemia | Tamponade. Explanation: Very wide pulse pressure, low diastolic pressure, steep upstroke and a lost notch (often a bisferiens double peak): aortic regurgitation. AS is the opposite — slow, small and late.

Where in the app: Lines › Challenge › Slow to rise
Content to review: An elderly patient with a systolic murmur. The arterial upstroke is slow, with a shoulder on the way up, and peaks late. Answer: Aortic stenosis. Other options: Aortic regurgitation | Septic shock | Stiff arteries only. Explanation: Pulsus parvus et tardus — a small, late, slow-rising pulse with an anacrotic shoulder — is aortic stenosis.

Where in the app: Lines › Challenge › Is she fluid-responsive?
Item: What do you make of the PPV?
Content to review: Ventilated, MAP 80. The monitor shows a pulse-pressure variation over 30 %. The team suggests a fluid bolus. Answer: It cannot be used: the rhythm is irregular (AF). Other options: Over 13 % — give fluid | Over 13 % — start a vasopressor | It proves she is overloaded. Explanation: PPV needs a regular rhythm: in AF every beat has a different filling time, so the pulse pressure varies whatever the volume status. Use a passive leg raise or a fluid challenge with a cardiac-output measure instead.

Where in the app: Lines › Challenge › Resuscitate the bleeding patient
Item: Is this patient likely to respond to fluid?
Content to review: Haemorrhage, now controlled. Ventilated at 8 mL/kg, sinus tachycardia. Use the waveform to guide fluid. Answer: Yes — PPV > 13 % on controlled ventilation in sinus rhythm. Other options: No — the CVP is low | Cannot tell without a cuff pressure | No — the MAP is 65. Explanation: All the conditions for PPV are met and it is well above 13 %. Give fluid in 500 mL steps and re-check the variation after each.

Where in the app: Lines › Challenge › Warm, vasodilated and hypotensive
Item: What does the waveform suggest is the main problem?
Content to review: Septic shock after 2 L of fluid. MAP in the high 50s, low diastolic, low dicrotic notch. Answer: Low vascular tone — a vasopressor is needed. Other options: Pump failure — start an inotrope | Severe hypovolaemia only | Tamponade. Explanation: Low diastolic pressure with a notch near the diastolic level and a high heart rate: vasoplegia. Norepinephrine restores tone. PPV is still just above 13 %, so some fluid may help alongside it.
